lesson_title: A Ramp That Moves and a Lever That Spins
hook_text: An axe is a ramp. A doorknob is a lever. Both of them have been fooling you.
clip_script: Two of the oldest machines on Earth are hiding in your kitchen. First, the wedge. A ramp lets you push something heavy up slowly. Turn the ramp round and drive it into the thing instead, and you have an axe. Swing down, the thin edge goes in, the thick sides shove the log apart. Your downward push becomes a huge sideways split. Thinner edge, bigger advantage; that is why a sharp knife slices and a blunt one squashes. Second, the wheel and axle. A big wheel stuck to a thin rod. Turn the wheel gently and the rod turns hard: tap, doorknob, screwdriver. It is a lever bent into a circle, pivot at the centre. Turn the rod instead and the rim flies: that is your bicycle. Ramp that moves, lever that spins. You use both every single day.
visual_style: Whiteboard ramp tips over into an axe head entering a log with sideways arrows; then a wheel on a rod with a long rim arrow and a short axle arrow, morphing into a tap and then a bicycle wheel.
pacing: Two halves of thirty seconds, each with a definition, a demonstration and one everyday example.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and work out which way the wheel and axle in a bicycle is being used.
